web_blocks.text: The physical chain begins with fluorspar, which the company says it imports from multiple geographies including South Africa, Thailand, Vietnam and Kenya, and sulphur, sourced domestically. Sulphuric acid is made at the site and used in HF production; HF then moves into AHF/DHF grades and downstream derivatives. The company also reports captive power supported by waste-heat recovery, dedicated acid tanks, an HF cylinder-filling station and effluent-treatment infrastructure at its 60-acre Cuddalore complex. [1][2]

The plant’s position near Chennai Port supports inbound raw-material logistics and export shipments. TANFAC reports more than 105 clients across more than ten countries, with FY26 sales about 95% domestic and 5% export. The supplied public materials identify customer types and some long-term supply arrangements but do not describe distributor margins, route-to-market economics, customer concentration by product or named confidential buyers. Management says raw-material cost pass-through in contracts can lag input changes by roughly 30–45 days; ICRA separately flags spread, working-capital and hazardous-HF transport risks. [1][2][3][6][7]

One practical, illustrative chain is a solar-grade DHF shipment to a qualified photovoltaic-wafer producer: TANFAC converts captive HF into the high-purity grade, the customer qualifies samples, and contracted deliveries are scheduled against the disclosed order book. Another illustrative chain is HFC-32 supply to an HVAC buyer after commissioning and qualification. These describe plausible end-to-end archetypes from disclosed product uses and project information; they are not named customer cases or claims about individual shipments. [1][2][6]

web_blocks.caption: Audited FY26 standalone ₹ crore waterfall. COGS is cost of materials consumed plus the reported inventory change; other operating expense combines power and fuel with other expenses. CFO is net cash from operating activities. Capex is cash purchase of property, plant and equipment, including CWIP movements and capital advances/creditors, not total investing cash flow. [1]
web_blocks.takeaway: FY26 record revenue translated into ₹43.4 crore operating cash flow against ₹70.1 crore profit after tax; audited PPE cash outflow was ₹82.4 crore as the company expanded capacity. The cash story is therefore one of earnings, working-capital absorption and deliberate build-out—not simply the income statement. [1]

web_blocks.title: The ₹100 lens
paragraphs: The waterfall block contains the audited, period-matched annual values only. The compiler should calculate the per-₹100 rows; do not substitute quarterly or half-year cash flow into the FY26 annual bridge. [1]

web_blocks.text: A practical supply-chain map has three upstream questions: where feedstocks come from, what TANFAC controls itself, and what it must move safely to customers. Company materials identify fluorspar from South Africa, Thailand, Vietnam and Kenya, with sulphur sourced domestically; the FY26 investor presentation also identifies Chennai Petroleum Corporation Limited as a sulphur supplier and describes a multi-geography fluorspar supplier base. HF is made in-house from fluorspar and captive sulphuric acid. The integrated site uses captive power and waste-heat recovery for a large share of energy needs. This reduces dependence on some merchant inputs, but not on imported mineral supply, shipping schedules or energy reliability. [1][2]

web_blocks.text: The customer interface is less visible than the factory. The company reports more than 105 clients across more than ten countries and has disclosed long-term solar-grade DHF and refrigerant-gas arrangements. It has also said confidentiality restrictions prevent naming some customers. The filings do not say whether every product is sold directly, whether agents are used in particular regions, what share of volume is spot versus formula-based by product, or how transport and packaging costs are allocated. Avoid filling those gaps with a generic “direct sales” assumption. The reported mechanisms are narrower: certain products are covered by long-term contracts, and selected contracts reset raw-material-linked terms with a lag. [1][3][6]

A customer-delivery archetype can nevertheless be traced without pretending to know an undisclosed buyer. A solar-wafer manufacturer identifies a need for high-purity etching and cleaning; TANFAC uses in-house HF to produce solar-grade DHF, demonstrates the quality through customer trials, and fulfils orders that the company says cover about 85% of original annual capacity through FY29. For this grade, the company reports formula-based pricing that passes raw-material movements to the customer over a defined cycle; management describes a lag of about 30–45 days. Exact shipment cadence, product price, and buyer identity are not disclosed. The path is an evidence-backed process archetype, not an individual account history. [1][2][3][6]

A second archetype is a refrigerant buyer. The intended path begins with captive HF and purchased dichloromethane, proceeds through the planned HFC-32 process at Cuddalore, and ends with qualified supply to an HVAC/refrigeration customer. The company reports long-term arrangements for part of planned capacity and formula pass-through in the contracts, while ICRA notes that commissioning, cost, ramp-up and timely sales remain key monitorables. The latest call described construction progress and customer evaluations; the plant was not yet a proven operating channel in the evidence supplied. [1][3][6][7]

web_blocks.text: The waterfall is deliberately annual and audited. In FY26, ₹711.074 crore of operating revenue less ₹444.7329 crore of materials and inventory cost leaves the reported gross-profit base; employee expense, power/fuel and other expenses take operating EBITDA to ₹112.064 crore. Depreciation, finance cost, other income and tax then reconcile to roughly ₹70.143 crore of PAT, with minor rounding at the fourth decimal because reported statements are in lakhs. Separately, the cash-flow statement shows ₹43.4008 crore from operations and ₹82.4487 crore cash PPE purchases. The latter is not total investing cash flow, which also includes purchases and sales of investments. [1]

web_blocks.title: Logistics and working-capital counterfactual
paragraphs: If fluorspar lead times lengthen or freight routes are disrupted, buffer inventory may protect production but raise working-capital needs. If input costs move faster than contractual reset periods, revenue may reflect pass-through before margins normalize. If HF transport rules tighten, permits and specialized handling help but cannot eliminate the exposure. These are the exact mechanisms to monitor—not a generic claim that integration makes supply risk disappear. [1][6][7]

book_paragraphs: When you follow a molecule through this business, integration is tangible: sulphuric acid and HF are produced in-house, and HF is both a saleable product and the feedstock for downstream grades. The Cuddalore location, captive utilities, hazardous-material facilities and port access support that chain. Yet physical integration does not eliminate commercial friction. Sulphur and fluorspar costs can move before contractual pass-through catches up, and HF handling and transport carry regulatory and safety obligations that ICRA treats as material constraints. [1][2][7]

The audited FY26 cash bridge is a useful discipline against headline growth. Revenue from operations was ₹711.07 crore; net cash from operating activities was ₹43.40 crore, while profit after tax was ₹70.14 crore and cash purchases of property, plant and equipment were ₹82.45 crore. Working-capital changes consumed ₹52.84 crore before tax payments, and the company deployed cash into capacity. You should read growth, cash conversion and capex together: an integrated plant can create a stronger product platform while absorbing substantial cash during expansion. [1]

Walk the chain from the supplier’s shipment to the customer’s process. Fluorspar is imported from several countries; sulphur is sourced domestically. TANFAC converts those inputs into sulphuric acid and hydrofluoric acid, uses captive power and waste-heat recovery, and then sells or consumes HF in downstream chemistry. A solar-grade customer’s problem is not simply “buy acid”: it needs a specified high-purity grade that passes its own process qualification. TANFAC reports successful trials with an Indian wafer maker and contracted orders. That makes the example concrete without naming the buyer or inventing a shipment quantity. [1][2][3]

The refrigerant route has a different set of gates. The planned HFC-32 facility uses the company’s fluorine platform, but the full route also depends on dichloromethane supply, project completion, regulatory conditions, customer qualification and stable production. The latest call described substantial construction progress and evaluation work; ICRA explicitly identified commissioning within cost and schedule, operating stabilization and timely ramp-up as monitorables. This is why you should label the refrigerant workflow “planned” until the facility is commissioned and repeat sales are evidenced. [1][6][7]

TANFAC’s control points are real but bounded. Captive sulphuric acid, in-house HF, site utilities and a single integrated location reduce some dependence on outside intermediates. The company has infrastructure for acid storage, cylinder filling, effluent treatment and emergency response, and ICRA notes a valid transport permit for HF. Yet imported fluorspar remains a logistics exposure; sulphur and fluorspar cost shifts can arrive before customer pass-through; hazardous transport can face scrutiny; and higher buffer stocks can tie up cash. Integration lowers selected risks, not all risks. [1][2][6][7]

The audited FY26 bridge makes the cash consequence visible. Materials and inventory changes, employee costs, energy and other expenses absorb much of each revenue rupee before depreciation and finance costs. Operating cash flow improved from FY25 but remained below PAT, while cash PPE purchases were larger than operating cash flow. The supply chain is therefore both a manufacturing advantage and a financing requirement: keeping feedstock available, paying for safe handling and completing new capacity all compete for cash. Use the annual statement, not a quarterly run rate, to understand that funding burden. [1]

The same discipline applies to logistics. The disclosed port proximity, import origins and domestic sulphur sourcing establish the broad transport architecture, while the acid tanks, filling station, emergency response and environmental systems show the site’s specialized handling requirements. The records do not reveal the carrier network, packaging mix by product, freight cost per tonne or customer delivery schedule. Your narrative can still be specific: raw materials arrive from a multi-origin chain, are converted at Cuddalore, and products move to domestic and export users under disclosed contract arrangements. It should stop before claiming a distribution model that the company has not described. [1][2][7]

In a chemical business, a buffer is neither automatically prudent nor automatically wasteful. TANFAC’s management said it raised fluorspar cover when shipping lead times and geopolitical disruptions created continuity concerns. The same call connected the higher inventory to a rise in payables and said the company expected the balance to move back toward normal cover as conditions allowed. That is a management explanation, not a completed normalization. Later filings should show whether inventory days and creditor days recede together, whether production continues without interruption, and whether the cash conversion cycle returns toward the FY26 level. [1][6]

A useful cash-flow distinction is between operating costs recognized in the income statement and cash tied up in timing. The audited FY26 statement records an inventory-related credit in calculating cost of materials and separately shows working-capital uses across receivables, inventories and payables. The result is that gross profit and CFO answer different questions: gross profit describes production economics under accounting recognition, while CFO also reflects collection, stockholding, supplier terms and tax payments. The company’s H1 buffer-stock explanation makes this difference especially relevant. You should not infer that a strong production quarter immediately translates into equivalent operating cash. [1][6]

The delivery mechanism deserves the same evidentiary care as the production route. Formula pass-through is disclosed for long-term contracts, with raw-material movements transferred over a defined cycle; management describes a lag of roughly 30–45 days for certain input changes. This can reduce long-term spread exposure while leaving timing exposure between purchases and customer resets. The contract is therefore not a guarantee of unchanged quarterly margins. Nor does the public information show that every product and every buyer has identical terms. The defensible statement is that some contracted arrangements include formula-based pass-through, with an observed lag described by management. [1][3][6][7]

book_callouts.title: Reflection — follow cash alongside molecules
book_callouts.text: Where did the operating cash go in FY26: into working capital, tax, or plant construction? The audited cash-flow statement answers more than a revenue chart does. Keep its annual period intact when comparing it with profits or capex. [1]
